hints: Check each carbon for four different attached groups, look especially for a carbon joined to H, a methyl group and two different larger fragments.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
Picture each carbon with its four bonds. A chiral centre must have four completely different groups. $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{C=O}$ carbons can never be chiral because they have duplicate H or duplicate bonds.

Spot the only candidate**
In T, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}( \text{CH}_3)\text{COCH}_3$, the CH is joined to H, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ and $\text{COCH}_3$. That is four different groups, so it is chiral. In P, Q, R and S every aliphatic carbon is $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2$ or $\text{CH}$ with two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so none is chiral.
Final answer: Asterisk (*) on the CH carbon of T only, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}^*( \text{CH}_3)\text{COCH}_3$. No other chiral centres in P, Q, R or S.

hints: Count the peaks in Fig. 8.1 and match splitting to structure, a singlet near $\delta = 3.7$, a quartet near $\delta = 2.5$ and a triplet near $\delta = 1.0$ points to an isolated $\text{CH}_2$ plus an ethyl group.
Compare R $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with Q and S, only one isomer has both a $\text{CH}_2$ with no neighbouring H and a separate $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ fragment.
walkthrough:
Read the spectrum like a detective**
You have $\delta = 7.2$ for the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ protons, a singlet at $\delta = 3.7$ integrating to 2H, a quartet at $\delta = 2.5$ integrating to 2H, and a triplet at $\delta = 1.0$ integrating to 3H. The quartet plus triplet pair is the classic fingerprint of a $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ ethyl group.

Fit the ethyl plus singlet pattern to R**
Only R, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, contains both a $\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ ethyl ketone fragment and a separate benzylic $\text{CH}_2$. The $\text{CH}_2$ next to phenyl and carbonyl is deshielded to $\delta = 3.7$, the $\text{CH}_2$ next to carbonyl alone appears at $\delta = 2.5$, and the $\text{CH}_3$ of the ethyl group appears at $\delta = 1.0$.

Final answer: Compound R, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Displayed formula with labels: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\mathbf{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ gives $\delta = 3.7$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CO}\mathbf{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ gives $\delta = 2.5$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\mathbf{CH}_3$ gives $\delta = 1.0$.

hints: Recall that splitting is caused only by protons on the immediately adjacent carbon atoms, so examine what is attached to both sides of the $\delta = 3.7$ $\text{CH}_2$ group.
walkthrough:
See why no splitting occurs**
The $\delta = 3.7$ peak is the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\mathbf{CH}_2\text{CO}$ protons. On one side is the ipso carbon of the benzene ring which carries no H, on the other side is the carbonyl carbon $\text{C=O}$ which also carries no H. With n = 0 neighbouring protons, n+1 = 1, so a singlet is observed.
Final answer: Singlet, because there are no H atoms on the neighbouring C atoms.

hints: A doublet means n = 1, so look for a $\text{CH}_3$ group next to a single CH proton in the list P to T.
walkthrough:
Hunt for a methyl next to one proton**
A doublet needs a group with exactly one neighbour H. In P, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups are next to one CH, so they appear as a doublet. In T, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COCH}_3$, the $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)$ methyl is next to one CH, so it also gives a doublet.

hints: Count distinct proton environments, remembering all five benzene H count as one environment and equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups count as one.
walkthrough:
Count environments to get to three**
P, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, has $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ as one peak, the CH as a second peak, and the two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups as a third peak. All other isomers have four or more proton environments because their alkyl protons are all non equivalent.

hints: Think why an ordinary solvent like water or hexane would ruin a proton NMR spectrum and what property the solvent must have.
walkthrough:
Choose a silent solvent**
The solvent must not give its own proton signal and must dissolve the ketone. $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains D not H so it is invisible in proton NMR, while $\text{CCl}_4$ contains no H at all. Both also provide a deuterium lock signal for the spectrometer.

hints: Recall which functional groups disappear on shaking with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ and check whether compound T contains any of them.
walkthrough:
See why D2O does nothing here**
Shaking with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ only removes peaks due to $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ protons, which exchange to form $\text{O-D}$ or $\text{N-D}$. T, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COCH}_3$, is a ketone with only $\text{C-H}$ protons attached to carbon and phenyl. These do not exchange, so all peaks remain with the same chemical shift, splitting and integration.
Final answer: No difference, T has no exchangeable protons ($\text{OH}$ or $\text{NH}$) to exchange with D.

hints: For each disubstituted benzene, use the symmetry plane to decide which ring carbons are equivalent, then add the side chain carbons.
Remember ethylbenzene has no symmetry in the ring beyond pairs, while para xylene is the most symmetrical with only two distinct ring carbon types.
walkthrough:
Count ethylbenzene and meta xylene**
Ethylbenzene has four ring environments (ipso, ortho pair, meta pair, para) plus $\text{CH}_2$ plus $\text{CH}_3$, total 6. For 1,3-dimethylbenzene, the ring gives C1/C3, C2, C4/C6, C5 (4 types) plus one methyl type for the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups, total 5.

Count ortho and para xylene**
For 1,2-dimethylbenzene, the ring gives C1/C2, C3/C6, C4/C5 (3 types) plus one methyl type, total 4. For 1,4-dimethylbenzene, high symmetry gives only C1/C4 and C2/C3/C5/C6 (2 ring types) plus one methyl type, total 3.
Final answer: Ethylbenzene (top left): 6 peaks. 1,3-dimethylbenzene (top right): 5 peaks. 1,2-dimethylbenzene (bottom left): 4 peaks. 1,4-dimethylbenzene (bottom right): 3 peaks.
